Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 31
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Professor
  trauma_type: Life-threatening motor vehicle collision
  pcl5: 67

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Dissociative Feeling: Beginning to feel detached or unreal, Crash Discussions: Talk about accidents, Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident
  Threat: Waking Alert: I wake during the night to check whether I am safe, Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
  Memory: Cannot Explain Clearly: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish, Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together, Partial Clarity: Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Happiness: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable., Belong Nowhere: I no longer belong anywhere, Lost Meaning: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore

Vignette:
Malia, a 31-year-old married professor of Oceania background, sought treatment after nearly a year of living with the aftermath of a life-threatening motor vehicle collision that had left her feeling unlike herself in ways she could not ignore. Before the crash, she had understood her life as busy but steady: teaching, preparing lectures, and sharing an ordinary domestic routine with her husband. The collision happened on a day she had been driving home from work, when another car struck hers with enough force to make the scene feel instantly chaotic and wrong. She remembered the violent impact, the sudden loss of control, and the terrifying sense that her body and surroundings were no longer responding as they should. In the weeks that followed, she found that her recollection of the event did not settle into a single coherent story. When she tried to explain it to other people, including her husband and later her doctor, she would lose the thread partway through and stop, frustrated by the way the account slipped away from her. Some parts of the crash stood out with painful clarity—the instant of impact, the sound, the sense of being hit—while other sections were blank, leaving her with disconnected pieces that never quite fit together.

As time went on, certain moments began to bring the event back with unusual force. If coworkers talked casually about accidents, traffic, or someone else’s close call, Malia would feel an abrupt internal shift, as if the world had gone slightly distant and unreal. She described those moments as beginning with a detached feeling that made her uneasy before she could even place why. Seeing cars that had been hit in accidents had a similar effect. On her commute, a damaged vehicle at the roadside could pull her attention so completely that she felt herself pulled back into the crash scene, as though the sight were not simply something in the present but a doorway into what had happened to her. These experiences were not just upsetting recollections; they carried the force of being suddenly back there, and she found herself acting as if danger were once again immediate.

At night, Malia’s sleep was broken by a different kind of vigilance. She woke often, sometimes without remembering what had stirred her, and checked whether she was safe. She would listen closely in the dark, alert to anything that might suggest the car, the road, or the possibility that something had gone wrong again. Even during the day she felt superalert and watchful, scanning her surroundings in a way that made ordinary environments exhausting. In lecture halls and hallways at the university, she noticed herself tracking sounds and movement rather than settling into the role that once felt natural to her. The vigilance was especially difficult during her workday, because the campus setting did not allow her to withdraw entirely; she had to stand at the front of classrooms and remain present with students while part of her attention stayed fixed on whether anything around her might signal threat.

Over time, Malia came to describe herself in increasingly bleak terms. She said that she used to be a happy person but now felt miserable most of the time, a statement she made with an almost disappointed disbelief, as though she were describing someone she no longer recognized. She also spoke of a painful sense that she no longer belonged anywhere. This was not limited to one setting: at home, she felt separate from her husband in a way she could not easily explain, and at work she felt as though she occupied her role by habit rather than by any genuine sense of place. She also said that nothing in her life felt meaningful anymore, including the career to which she had once devoted so much energy. The work itself continued, but it no longer carried the same purpose for her; days felt emptied out, as if the future that had once seemed open and organized now had no clear shape.

By the time she first sought help, the accumulation of these experiences had become impossible to dismiss. Malia was not asking for a quick return to how things had been, because she no longer trusted that such a return was possible. What brought her in was the growing fear that the detached moments, the night waking, and the sense of being on guard would keep narrowing her life until nothing felt familiar or worth holding onto. What she wanted most was not simply relief from the crash reminders, but some way to feel like herself again—to be able to describe what happened without losing the story, to move through a day without constantly checking for danger, and to believe that her life still had meaning.
